prompt: What subnet mask does /24 mean?

options.why: The number after the slash is how many bits are fixed for the network. 24 ones then 8 zeros, written as four bytes, is 255.255.255.0.
That is /16, which fixes only 16 bits.
That is /8, which fixes only the first byte.
That is /32, a single address with no room for a network at all.

hint: Count the bits: how many 1s before the 0s start?

prompt: How many usable host addresses does a /26 subnet have?

options.why: /26 leaves 6 host bits, so 2 to the power 6 = 64 addresses. Two are reserved, the network address and the broadcast address, leaving 62.
That is the total number of addresses. Two of them can never be given to a device.
This takes away only one reserved address. Both the network and the broadcast address are reserved.
26 is the number of network bits, not a count of hosts.

hint: 32 bits in all. How many are left for hosts, and how many of those are reserved?

prompt: A device has the address 192.168.1.70 with a /26 mask. What is the network address of its subnet?

options.why: A /26 splits the last byte into blocks of 64: 0, 64, 128, 192. The address 70 falls in the block that starts at 64.
That is the first block. 70 is past 63, so it is in the second one.
That is the device itself. A network address is the first address of its block.
That is the third block, which starts above 70.

hint: A /26 cuts the last number into steps of 64. Which step does 70 land in?

prompt: A device has the address 192.168.1.70 with a /26 mask. What is the broadcast address of its subnet?

options.why: The block runs from 64 to 127. The broadcast address is always the LAST address of the block, so 127.
That is the broadcast of the block BELOW, which runs 0 to 63.
That would be the broadcast for a /24. A /26 is four times smaller.
That is the last USABLE host. The broadcast sits one above it.

hint: The block starts at 64 and holds 64 addresses. Where does it end?

prompt: In the network 10.1.1.0/24, what is the first address you can give to a device?

options.why: 10.1.1.0 is the network address and cannot be used by a device. The next one up, .1, is the first that can.
That is the network address itself. It names the network, not a device.
Only ONE address is reserved at the start. .1 is free.
That is the broadcast address, which is reserved and sits at the end.

hint: The very first address of a network has a job already.

prompt: How many usable host addresses does a /30 subnet have?

options.why: /30 leaves 2 host bits, so 4 addresses. Take away the network and broadcast addresses and 2 are left. That is why /30 is used for a link between two routers.
That is the total. Two of the four are always reserved.
A link needs an address at each end, and /30 does give two.
30 counts network bits, not hosts.

hint: Only 2 bits are left for hosts. Then take 2 away.

prompt: How many /27 subnets fit inside one /24 network?

options.why: Going from /24 to /27 borrows 3 bits, and 2 to the power 3 is 8. Each /27 holds 32 addresses, and 8 x 32 = 256.
That is how many /26 subnets fit. /27 is one step smaller again.
3 is the number of bits borrowed, not the number of subnets. You must raise 2 to that power.
32 is how many ADDRESSES each /27 holds, not how many subnets there are.

hint: How many bits do you borrow going from 24 to 27? Then 2 to that power.

prompt: How many bits long is an IPv4 address?

options.why: An IPv4 address is four bytes, and each byte is 8 bits. 4 x 8 = 32.
4 is the number of parts separated by dots. Each part is a whole byte.
No version of IP uses 64 bits. IPv4 is 32 and IPv6 is 128.
That is IPv6, which was made much longer because IPv4 addresses ran out.

hint: Four numbers, one byte each. How many bits in a byte?

prompt: Is the address 10.0.0.5 a private address or a public one?

options.why: Everything starting 10. is private. The three private ranges are 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x and 192.168.x.x. They are used inside homes and offices and are never routed on the internet.
A public address can be reached from the internet. No 10.x.x.x address ever can.

options.text: It depends on the subnet mask
options.why: The mask decides how the network is split. Whether an address is private is decided by the address itself.
A broadcast address is the last one in its block. .5 is an ordinary host address.

hint: There are three ranges kept back for use inside a building.

verify.program:
import ipaddress
a = ipaddress.ip_address("10.0.0.5")
print("Private" if a.is_private else "Public")

prompt: Which one of these is NOT a private address?

options.why: The private block in the 172 range is only 172.16 to 172.31. 172.32 is just past the end of it, so it is public.
This is the FIRST address of the 172 private block, so it is private.
The whole of 192.168.x.x is private. This is the usual address of a home router.
Every 10.x.x.x address is private, right up to the end of the range.

hint: The 172 private block does not cover every 172. Where does it stop?

verify.program:
import ipaddress
candidates = ["172.32.5.1", "172.16.5.1", "192.168.0.1", "10.255.255.254"]
public = [c for c in candidates if not ipaddress.ip_address(c).is_private]
print(public[0] if len(public) == 1 else f"not unique: {public}")

prompt: Which port does HTTPS use by default?

options.why: HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS, and it was given its own port, 443.
That is plain HTTP, with no encryption.
That is SSH, for logging in to a machine remotely.
That is a common port for a test web server, but it is not the default for HTTPS.

hint: HTTP is 80. The secure one is a different number.

prompt: Which port does SSH use by default?

options.why: SSH, the secure way to log in to a machine over a network, is port 22.
That is FTP, the old file transfer protocol, which sends passwords in plain text.
That is Telnet. SSH replaced Telnet because Telnet is not encrypted.
That is SMTP, for sending email.

hint: It sits right between FTP and Telnet.

prompt: Which port does DNS normally use?

options.why: DNS uses port 53. It usually runs over UDP because a lookup is one small question and one small answer.
That is HTTP. DNS runs before the web request, to find the address first.
That is DHCP, which hands out addresses. DNS looks names up.
That is HTTPS, the port a browser uses for a secure page. DNS runs before that request, to find the address to connect to.

hint: It is a low number, below 60.

prompt: A server is listening on TCP port 21. Which service is that, by default?

options.why: Port 21 is FTP, the old file transfer protocol. It sends the username and password in plain text, which is why it is avoided today.
SSH is port 22, one higher.
SMTP, for sending mail, is port 25.
HTTP is port 80.

hint: It is the one just below SSH, and it moves files.

prompt: What does the HTTP status code 404 mean?

options.why: The server was reached and it understood the request, but there is nothing at that address.
That is 403. The page exists but you are not allowed to see it.
That is 500, where the server itself broke.
That is 400, where the request was malformed.

hint: The most famous error on the web.

prompt: What does the HTTP status code 500 mean?

options.why: Something broke on the SERVER side. The request was fine, so sending it again usually changes nothing.
That is 404, and it is a 4xx, which means the problem is on the client side.
That is 503, which usually means the server is overloaded or down for maintenance.
That is 401, where you need to log in first.

hint: Codes starting with 5 point the finger at one side. Which one?

prompt: What does the HTTP status code 301 mean?

options.why: The page has a new address for good. Browsers and search engines remember the new one and stop asking for the old.
That is 302, a TEMPORARY move. Nothing is remembered, so the old address is tried again next time.
That is 304, which tells the browser its cached copy is still good.
That is 201, usually the answer to a POST that made something new.

hint: There are two redirects, 301 and 302. One is forever.

prompt: Which range of HTTP status codes means the CLIENT made the mistake?

options.why: The 400s blame the request: not found, forbidden, bad request. Sending the same request again will not help.
The 500s blame the server. The request was fine, so trying again later may work.
The 200s mean success. Nothing went wrong at all.
The 300s are redirects. The page has moved, which is nobody’s mistake.

hint: Which group holds 404 and 403?

verify.program:
from http import HTTPStatus
ranges = {"1xx": 100, "2xx": 200, "3xx": 301, "4xx": 404, "5xx": 500}
hits = [k for k, c in ranges.items() if HTTPStatus(c).is_client_error]
print(hits[0] if len(hits) == 1 else f"not unique: {hits}")

prompt: In the OSI model, which layer does the IP protocol belong to?

options.why: IP carries a packet from one network to another using addresses. Choosing a path between networks is exactly what layer 3 does.
Layer 2 moves frames between devices on the SAME local network, using MAC addresses. It cannot cross between networks.
Layer 4 is TCP and UDP. They sit on top of IP and look after the conversation, not the address.
Layer 7 is where HTTP and DNS live, right next to the program the user sees.

hint: Which layer is named after the thing IP addresses identify?

prompt: A normal network switch works at which OSI layer?

options.why: A switch reads MAC addresses and sends each frame out of the one port where that device sits. MAC addresses are layer 2.
That is a hub or a cable. A hub copies the signal to every port because it reads no addresses at all.
That is a router, which reads IP addresses and joins different networks together.
Layer 4 is TCP and UDP, which are handled by the two computers, not by the box in the middle.

hint: Which kind of address does a switch read?

prompt: Which is true about TCP compared with UDP?

options.text: TCP checks that data arrived and resends what was lost
options.why: TCP numbers every piece, waits for the other side to confirm, and sends again if a confirmation never comes. That makes it reliable but slower.

options.text: TCP is faster because it does not wait
options.why: That is UDP. UDP just fires the data off, which is why it suits live video and games where a late piece is useless anyway.

options.text: TCP sends data without making a connection first
options.why: That is UDP again. TCP always sets up a connection first, with the three-way handshake.
Both TCP and UDP use port numbers. That is how one machine runs many services at once.

hint: One of the two promises delivery. Which one, and what does that promise cost?

prompt: What is the order of the TCP three-way handshake?

options.why: The client asks to start (SYN). The server agrees and asks back in one message (SYN-ACK). The client confirms (ACK). Now both sides know the other can hear them.
You cannot confirm something before it has been asked. The first message must be the SYN.
The server saves a round trip by combining its agreement and its own request into one SYN-ACK.
The server does send its own SYN, but it is bundled with the ACK, which is why there are three steps and not four.

hint: Three messages, and the middle one does two jobs at once.

prompt: What is the job of DNS?

options.text: It turns a name such as example.com into an IP address
options.why: Computers route by numbers, but people remember names. DNS is the phone book that turns one into the other.

options.text: It hands out an IP address to a device that joins the network
options.why: That is DHCP. DNS does not give out addresses, it looks them up.

options.text: It encrypts traffic between a browser and a server
options.why: That is TLS, the S in HTTPS.

options.text: It lets many devices share one public address
options.why: That is NAT, which your home router does.

hint: Think of it as the phone book of the internet.

prompt: What is the job of DHCP?

options.text: It gives a device an IP address automatically when it joins
options.why: Without DHCP somebody would have to type an address into every phone and laptop by hand, and make sure no two were the same.

options.text: It turns a website name into an IP address
options.why: That is DNS. DHCP hands addresses out, DNS looks them up.

options.text: It decides the best path between two networks
options.why: That is routing, done by routers using their routing tables.

options.text: It checks that data arrived safely
options.why: That is TCP, at the transport layer.

hint: Why does your phone get an address the moment it joins the wifi?

prompt: What does NAT do on a home router?

options.text: It lets many private addresses share one public address
options.why: Every device at home has a private address. The router swaps that for its single public address on the way out, and remembers which reply belongs to which device. This is a big part of why IPv4 has lasted so long.

options.text: It gives each device at home its own public address
options.why: The opposite. There are not enough public IPv4 addresses for that, which is the problem NAT solves.

options.text: It encrypts everything leaving the house
options.why: NAT only rewrites addresses. Encryption is TLS, and it is a separate job.
That is DNS, which turns a name into an address. NAT works on the addresses themselves, after DNS has done its job.

hint: How do ten devices at home get online through one address from the internet company?
